findings.observation: The source prints f(x)=x³=1 instead of x³−1.
findings.resolution: Read f(x)=x³−1; the original fraction and subsequent derivatives show that intention.
findings.independent_derivation: f(1)=0 is required; x³ by itself is1 atx=1 and would not yield the intended0/0 form.

findings.observation: The source writes lim(cosx−1)/x=lim(−sinx)/x=0. The middle limit is−1, not0.
findings.resolution: The derivative of denominatorx is1: lim(−sinx)/1=0.
findings.independent_derivation: Independently,(cosx−1)/x=−2sin²(x/2)/x→0, whereas−sinx/x→−1. The final answer0 is correct only after fixing the intermediate denominator.

findings.observation: The second numerator is printed c²e^(ax) even though the parameter throughout is a.
findings.independent_derivation: Repeated differentiation gives d^k e^(ax)/dx^k=a^k e^(ax); the tenth derivative a^10e^(ax) is printed correctly.

findings.location: Full LHopital usage after easy version
findings.observation: Only the easy pointwise version is derived. The general rule is demonstrated without a complete hypothesis statement. An indeterminate-looking form alone does not authorize differentiation.
findings.resolution: On a one-sided punctured interval require differentiable f,g, g-prime nonzero there, an appropriate0/0 or infinity/infinity limit, and existence of lim f-prime/g-prime as a finite value or signed infinity. Apply separately to both sides for a two-sided limit. Check the hypotheses at every repetition.
findings.independent_derivation: For the easy version, differentiability at a plus f(a)=g(a)=0 and g-prime(a)≠0 suffices via the two difference quotients. For a finite0/0 endpoint, continuous extension and Cauchy mean value theorem give f(x)/g(x)=f-prime(c)/g-prime(c) for c betweenx and endpoint; the derivative-ratio limit then supplies the result. The source does not prove the full infinity variants.

findings.observation: The source writes x→0 before noting growth as x→0+. Its deliberately wrong second differentiation is correctly rejected later; this is an instructional counterexample, not an endorsed zero answer.
findings.resolution: State right limit+∞, left limit−∞, hence no two-sided limit. The first derivative ratio also has no two-sided extended limit, so the two-sided rule cannot certify the displayed equality as a value.
findings.independent_derivation: sinx/x²=(sinx/x)/x, with sinx/x→1. cosx/(2x) has the same opposing one-sided signs; once numerator tends1, it is not0/0 and a second application is invalid.

findings.observation: The source says it does not know how to find lim1/lnx near0. This auxiliary limit is immediate and is not an obstacle to recognizing0/0.
findings.resolution: As x→0+, ln x→−∞, so1/lnx→0. The alternative is valid but gives a less convenient derivative ratio−x(lnx)².
findings.independent_derivation: The chosen quotient ln x/(1/x) gives derivative ratio−x→0. For the alternative, set t=−lnx→∞; x(lnx)²=t²e^(−t)→0 by the already established exponential growth comparison.

findings.observation: Trigonometric calculations use radians. Positive a is stated for growth; x>0 is required for logarithms, real tenth-root simplification and x^x definition.
findings.resolution: For x^x take the one-sided x→0+ limit. Interpret ≪ as ratio→0, and0/0,1^∞,0^0 as classifications of limits rather than assigned numerical values.
findings.independent_derivation: f(x)=f(a)+f-prime(a)(x−a)+o(x−a) justifies the linear ratios when denominator slope is nonzero; cosx=1−x²/2+o(x²) justifies Example5. With a>0, e^(ax)/x^n→∞ for fixed nonnegative integern, while ln x/x^b→0 for b>0.

findings.observation: Correct target answers are3/2,5,3,sqrt2,0,−1/2; Example6 has opposite infinite one-sided limits. Growth and x^x conclusions are correct.
findings.resolution: Polynomial factorization and trigonometric identities independently confirm the finite limits; substituting x=e^(−t) verifies x ln x→0 and then x^x→1 by continuity of exp.
findings.independent_derivation: (x^15−1)/(x³−1)=1+x³+x^6+x^9+x^12→5. The shifted trig quotient is a difference quotient with derivative cos(π/4)+sin(π/4)=sqrt2. (cosx−1)/x²=−(1/2)[sin(x/2)/(x/2)]²→−1/2.

technical_disposition: Three confirmed notation/algebra defects appear in intermediate lines. The examples largely have correct target values; the sinx/x² case requires one-sided wording. The source does not present a full theorem statement or infinity-case proof, so complete sufficient hypotheses and the limit domains are recorded separately.
unresolved_limits: No full proof of the general infinity-form LHopital theorem is present in this packet; it is used as a theorem, while the easy version is proved.
